video.title: Start an Online Business With Just a Prompt

summary: The Koerner Office host Chris Koerner interviews Bolt.new co-founder and CEO Eric Simons about the product, how customers use it, and how to build with AI coding tools. Simons describes Bolt as a browser-based tool for turning prompts into web and mobile apps, with payments and APIs, and shares examples including client dashboards, CRMs, course sites, and niche apps. He explains Bolt’s launch, organic growth, and prompting practices such as starting with the interface, then adding functionality in smaller steps. The key takeaway is that fast, low-cost software creation makes it easier to test ideas, but more complex products still require planning, debugging, and technical understanding.

ideas.name: Bolt.new AI app-building platform
ideas.one_liner: An AI agent that turns ideas into web and mobile applications in a browser.
ideas.customer: Entrepreneurs, non-developers, developers, designers, product managers, sales and marketing teams, and existing businesses.
ideas.problem: Building software has required coding knowledge and work to set up development environments, functionality, payments, and APIs.
ideas.offer: A browser-based AI agent for building web and mobile applications, including websites, SaaS applications, APIs, and payment functionality.

price_points.label: Bolt can be tried for free, according to Eric.

pricing.notes: The transcript does not state Bolt's regular pricing.

acquisition_channels.details: The launch was announced with a carefully revised tweet thread and a demo video.

quote.text: We put together a tweet. Like that was I was hoping you'd say that.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

acquisition_channels.details: The team had built a community and a following on its account before the product launch.
Users shared apps they had built and deployed, which Eric described as the main way people still discover Bolt.

ideas.delivery: The user enters a prompt in the browser. Bolt generates an application, which can be edited, deployed, and connected to payments and APIs. Mobile apps can be previewed on a device through Expo.
unit_economics_claims: Eric says the company reached $700,000 in ARR with its earlier developer IDE after seven years.
Eric says Bolt went from zero to $20 million ARR in its first two months.
Before launch, the team hoped to add $100,000 ARR within a year.
Eric says the launch used zero dollars of paid marketing.
Eric says the project took about 90 days from development start to launch.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Eric says users could go from no website to accepting payments in five or ten minutes; time to the company's first revenue is not stated.

acquisition.how: Product demos, public posts, and users sharing deployed apps can bring in users with little routine manual work; people still create the launch content and maintain the community.

onboarding.how: Users can start in the prompt box and generate an app without a human onboarding call.

delivery.how: The software agent creates and deploys most of the product; users may need to guide it, check results, or debug.

billing.how: Software subscription billing could be automated, but Bolt's billing process is not described.

support.how: The team receives customer support emails and runs a Discord community; debugging and user questions can require people.

uk_applicability.notes: A browser-based software product can serve UK users in the same way. No UK-specific regulatory dependency is discussed.

risks: Generated software can break or produce the wrong result; Eric describes debugging as a real part of building.
Complex, uncommon features such as real-time driver dispatch require planning and may exceed what a prompt alone can handle.
The growth and ARR figures are the founder's claims and are not independently verified.

tactics.name: Launch with a clear tweet-thread FAQ
steps: Write a concise explanation of what the product is, why it is different, and which problem it solves.
Lead with a short demo and a hook that answers the first question prospective users are likely to ask.
Put supporting detail in later posts in the thread so interested readers can keep going.
Talk to friends and prospective customers to find their first objections before writing the launch message.
Revise the lead post until every phrase earns its place.

quote.text: the first tweet is the thing that needs to grab people's attention and be like, "Hey, this is a thing that sounds dope and is relevant and it's something you would want, right?"
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Build community before the product that works
steps: Build an audience around the company while developing and testing products.
Keep the community so it can help distribute a future launch that finds a strong fit.
Use the audience to seed the first users; then let users share what they built.

quote.text: when you're building like a startup, you should always be building community around it because you never know which of your iterations is going to be the one that clicks.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Make the first product experience easy to share
steps: Let new users start directly in the product instead of making them work through a long marketing page.
Make it quick to produce and deploy something users can show other people.
Encourage users to share their live result through their existing channels.

quote.text: And so, people would deploy that URL. They' be like, "Wow, I have a website live on the internet."
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Build the interface before layering on complex functionality
steps: Start with a relatively simple prompt for the main page and static parts.
Adjust the layout, colours, and user experience until the general flow is right.
Add functionality in separate prompts so each change is easier to inspect or roll back.
Use discussion mode to plan a difficult feature or debug issue before asking the agent to change code.

quote.text: start with like something, you know, relatively simple like you start with like the homepage and start with maybe some of the, you know, just static parts of the application
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Use references and broad prompts for design
steps: Give the agent a concrete visual reference by attaching a screenshot.
Describe the desired theme or outcome in plain language.
For non-specialist design work, let the model propose an initial version rather than specifying every detail.

quote.text: if you have specific examples, you can actually just take screenshots, drop them into the chat, and it'll use that as reference then
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Plan and test when the agent gets stuck
steps: Use discussion mode to work through a debugging problem rather than repeatedly asking the build agent to guess.
Provide the information the agent asks for and test proposed explanations.
Use logs and codebase instrumentation when the problem persists.
Break down complicated features, discuss trade-offs, and clarify the intended user experience before implementation.

quote.text: it'll actually start instrumenting the codebase if things are still going wrong it'll start adding logs and etc
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Test a business idea and iterate quickly
steps: Use software generation to launch an initial version.
Get feedback from users as soon as possible.
Iterate based on what users actually do and say.

quote.text: you want to just be able to go and launch things, get feedback as fast as possible and iterate and adapt.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

tactics.name: Clone an expensive or awkward tool for a real need
steps: Look at software you already use that costs more or takes a bigger percentage cut than you think it should.
Try rebuilding the needed workflow for your own use.
If the replacement works for you, consider reselling it to others with the same need.

quote.text: Whatever software tool you use, replicate that in bolt. Worst case, you save money for yourself. Best case, you resell that to others.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Sell digital content on an owned site
steps: Compare the revenue share of hosted platforms with selling from a site you own.
Build a course or content site with payments and user logins.
Sell course or material access directly through that site.

lessons.lesson: Treat entrepreneurship as repeated cycles of launching, getting feedback, and iterating; more attempts can accelerate learning.

quote.text: you want to just be able to go and launch things, get feedback as fast as possible and iterate and adapt.

lessons.lesson: Start with a customer problem and a clear reason the product should exist; ask prospective users what they would question.

quote.text: you have to talk to people to kind of get a sense of like what is that? What's the first thing people are going to ask you?
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: A concise launch message should explain the product's difference and value, with the most useful hook up front.

quote.text: having, you know, a very wellthoughtout hook and explanation of, you know, what this thing is, why it deserves to exist, why it's going to solve your problems.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: Build a community before you know which product iteration will succeed, so there is an audience ready to hear about it.

quote.text: you should always be building community around it because you never know which of your iterations is going to be the one that clicks.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: For many products, launch a useful version and improve it from real feedback instead of waiting for every feature to be polished.

quote.text: If the value you're providing is actually insanely great, which it should be, like that's the that's what you have to do, right?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Solve a problem you understand or are curious about; the guest says his strongest work came from a real need he wanted to address.

quote.text: the best things that I've ever done in my career have always been things where it's been like intrinsically I'm like this would be kind of cool.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: Keep technical knowledge where it helps you guide agents and understand how services fit together, especially as projects become more complex.

quote.text: understanding how this how software works, how to build software gives you just so much more leverage on how to actually control and use AI tools and agents
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: Use discussion and planning for complex functionality; software projects need a clear design for how the product should work.

quote.text: you have to do a lot of planning to kind of really think through okay how is this going to work what's the actual you know intended you know experience we're delivering here
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: Focus effort on the core customer value; design polish is useful, but it should match the reason the product will win.

quote.text: you should be just be focusing on solving the end user's problems, you know.
quote.speaker: Eric Simons

lessons.lesson: Making software easier to build can help people closest to a problem test solutions without needing to be experienced developers.
